title: Resolution looks to censure Madison alder amid harassment, assault allegations
text: Madison Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes Resize: Downtown Madison Capitol Isthmus Monona Terrace Lake Monona aerial  Digital Content Manager Downtown Madison Capitol Isthmus Monona Terrace Lake Monona aerial MADISON, Wis. -- A resolution slated to appear on the Madison Common Council's agenda next week calls for the censuring of Alder Charles Myadze. The resolution comes amid allegations of harassment and domestic violence against Myadze made by multiple women including current District 2 Alder Juliana Bennett and former Madison mayoral candidate and school board president Gloria Reyes. Speaking to News 3 Now last week, Bennett publicly accused Myadze of making inappropriate remarks about her body and clothing during a conference in March 2022 when she was only 22 years old. Bennett also alleged in her blog that Myadze locked her in his car in April 2022 and threatened her after learning that she had told three fellow alders about the incident. Reyes spoke to Madison365.com last week and alleged that Myadze once knocked her unconscious while the two were in an off-and-on relationship. An investigative report, released last week, could not find sufficient evidence proving Myadze violated the city's APM 3-5 harassment and discrimination policies, but Common Council President Yannette Figueroa Cole did say the report revealed "a troubling pattern of behavior." The resolution is authored by Alder MGR Govindarajan and is co-sponsored by seven alders, including Bennett, as well as Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. ​COPYRIGHT 2024 BY CHANNEL 3000. author: Arman Rahman
title: Complainant speaks out after report finds insufficient evidence that Madison alder violated harassment policy
text: Madison Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes Resize:  Reporter ​COPYRIGHT 2024 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. THIS MATERIAL MAY NOT BE PUBLISHED, BROADCAST, REWRITTEN OR REDISTRIBUTED. MADISON, Wis.- An investigation into Madison Alder Charles Myadze has found there is not enough evidence to say he committed acts of harassment that violate city policy and law. But one of the complainants from that report told News 3 Now she wanted to speak out, in hopes others will feel empowered to come forward. The 26-page report is the result of an investigation the city of Madison requested of OVB Law & Consulting S.C. After the city received three complaints alleging Myadze violated Administrative Procedure Memorandum No. 3-5, which outlines the city's policies surrounding prohibited harassment and discrimination, the report did not find sufficient evidence to prove that he violated the city's harassment and discrimination policies. This was the first investigation completed under the Common Council's updated code of conduct, which was adopted in July. According to City of Madison officials, since no violations were sustained, the process outlined by the code of conduct is complete. “I don't think it was really just like the investigators, I think that they did their job the best that they could. I think it's more so an issue of a legal process that is written by and for abusers,” said District 2 Alder Juliana Bennett. Bennett identified herself publicly Thursday as one of the complainants, who filed a formal complaint with the city she said prompted the private investigation. Even though the investigation has ended, Bennett said the impact on her job hasn’t. “Being with him on council is a real challenge,” said Bennett. “When I see him, especially after filing the report and going through this process, I just feel so angry inside. I hate listening to him speak on the council floor. I hate listening to anything he has to say,” Bennett told News 3 Now Thursday. “Because of my experience and knowing what he's done to other people and a deep-seated belief he shouldn't be in that space to begin with.” Bennett says she was only 22 when Myadze allegedly made inappropriate comments to her about her body and her clothing on different occasions. According to one alleged incident in the report at a conference, Bennett “wore a moderately low-cut red jumpsuit and open-toed heels. Myadze allegedly commented, ‘You’re wearing open-toed shoes, I bet you’re wearing a lot less at [REDACTED] place,’ and advised her to ‘put those [boobs] away and save them for [REDACTED].’” “And ever since he's made that comment, I still have it, but I feel uncomfortable wearing it again,” said Bennett. In a public statement posted on the City of Madison website, Bennett said she repeatedly asked Myadze to stop at the conference. In the report, Bennett said she confided in others about the incidents, but she thinks Myadze found out. She stated when Myadze picked her up to give her a ride, he allegedly locked the car doors and confronted her and referenced rumors about her comments on his comments and behaviors, denying anything inappropriate. “I was alone in his car and he locked the doors on me and then got in my face and was like yelling at me and screaming at me and telling me if I ever hear this again, we're done, we're done,” Bennett said Thursday. “So I was very, very scared…I was truly afraid of like, what would happen if I said anything like, will he hit me? Will he drive the car off really fast and potentially hurt me?” In the report, Myadze denied that and almost all the allegations against him, as was recounted by the complainants. In their credibility assessments, investigators labeled every complainant as credible with some respective biases but “due to inconsistencies, potential avoidance, and clear personal interest in the outcome,” labeled Myadze “a less credible witness.” They concluded Myadze’s conduct “did not constitute violations of APM 3-5 or state and federal laws.” For the incidents Bennett identified herself as the complainant, Myadze’s conduct “was found to constitute harassment and created a hostile work environment, under APM 3-5, though it did not meet the criteria for violations under state and federal laws.” According to Bennett, “after reopening the investigation, they revised their findings, citing that I remained professional, despite his threats.” Common Council President Alder Yanette Figueroa Cole released a public statement on the investigation, saying it revealed "a troubling pattern of behavior" and "significant issues we must address." “It also uncovers an unwelcome pattern of bullying, repeated aggressive behaviors, and creating an unacceptable power imbalance,” said Figueroa Cole in her statement Wednesday. Bennett said she hopes her making her story public empowers others. “I know that in my position I hold this specific lens of power and privilege being an alder and seeing the other women that have that came forward, I knew I couldn't keep silent and wanted to use my position to elevate this whole issue,” she said. “So that's why I chose to do that. And secondly, because I know that with the rumor mill, there might be speculation about who happened and what happened. So it was important to me to tell my own story and not have others tell it for me.” “Other people have come to me and privately shared their experiences with Alder Myadze, which is again repeating that pattern of behavior. It's clear to me he will not stop doing this. And he I feel as though he cannot represent his constituents well at all, or the city of Madison residents.” Myadze released the following statement to News 3 Now Thursday through his attorney: When I learned in May of this year, that there had been complaints against me under the city of Madison’s Administrative Procedure Memo (APM) 3-5 governing harassment, I was troubled and surprised. I fully cooperated with the independent investigation into the various allegations, and I was pleased, though not surprised, that the investigator found that none of the complaints against me were sustained by the evidence. Under the APM 3-5 Resource Guide, when a complaint is not sustained, there is supposed to be a debrief with both the complainant(s) and the respondent, and then the “case is considered closed.” APM 3-5 Resource Guide, section 9. In this case, the Common Council President—under the guise of issuing a “public summary of the findings” . . . to provide the public with a clear understanding of the investigation’s outcomes and the Council’s processes—issued a 7-paragraph statement, with 5 of the 7 paragraphs devoted to inflammatory commentary intended to cast me in a negative light, and to suggest that the result of this investigation was due to a problem with the city’s policy, not with the credibility and substance of the complaints against me. The Council President’s statement was needlessly antagonistic, inflammatory, misleading, and irresponsible. I encourage anyone interested in understanding the allegations, investigation, and resulting findings to read the investigative reports for themselves. Redacted versions of the reports are public records. ​COPYRIGHT 2024 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. THIS MATERIAL MAY NOT BE PUBLISHED, BROADCAST, REWRITTEN OR REDISTRIBUTED. MADISON (WKOW) -- Several Madison alders and the mayor are sponsoring a resolution to censure another alder for "conduct unbecoming of an alder." According to a filing on the city's website, the resolution cites "concerning actions" by Alder Charles Myadze documented in a investigative report. The resolution claims the findings in that report "undermined confidence in his [Myadze's] ability to maintain the professional decorum expected of a public official." It cites an April 2022 incident accusing Myadze of creating a hostile work environment. Alder Juliana Bennett said in a blog post that Myadze cornered her in his car and threatened her. In a statement to 27 News, Myadze described the communication he had with Bennett at that time as professional. The resolution encourages Myadze "to consider the impact of his continued presence on the Common Council to ongoing City priorities and processes." The city opened an investigation into Myadze's behavior after three women accused him of domestic violence and sexual harassment. The investigation found insufficient evidence that he violated the city's policy on harassment. Myadze has not been criminally charged for any of the allegations against him, and he's denied misconduct claims. The resolution is scheduled to be on the agenda at the next Common Council meeting on Tuesday, Nov. 26. At the time of publication, nine alders were listed as sponsors: There are 20 alders on Madison's Common Council.
